children.text: anyacca kāñcanārarasaiḥ samasūtakagandhayoḥ kajjalī hemapatrāṇi lepayet
children.translated_text: And further: with the juices of kāñcanāra, one should smear gold leaves with a black paste of equal parts purified mercury and sulfur.
In an equal measure, in a measure equal to the gold; the rest is clear.

children.text: karasyāṅguṣṭhe yā dhamanī sā jīvasākṣiṇī jīvo'sti no veti bodhanī jñeyā ||
children.translated_text: The artery at the thumb of the hand is witness to life; it should be understood as indicating whether life is present or not.

children.text: budhais tacceṣṭayā mandasthiracalagāminyā kāyasya dehasya sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ ca jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: By its movement, whether slow, steady, or moving, the learned should know the body's ease and distress.

children.text: marutkope sati nāḍī jalaukāsarpayor gatiṃ gamanaṃ dhatte ||
children.translated_text: When wind is aggravated, the pulse assumes the movement, the gait, of a leech or a snake.
When bile is aggravated, the pulse assumes the movement of a house-sparrow, crow, or frog.
The kuliṅga is the house-sparrow; when phlegm is aggravated, it assumes the movement of a goose or pigeon.

children.text: nāḍī sannipātataḥ tridoṣaprakopataḥ lāvatittiravartikānāṃ gamanaṃ dhatte ||
children.translated_text: In sannipāta, the aggravation of all three doṣas, the pulse assumes the movement of a quail, partridge, or vartikā bird.

children.text: natvekasya jantorgatyā nāmnāṃ prakupitasya doṣasya bodho bhavedato dvitrijantūnāṃ gatiḥ darśitā yathā vikṛtimāpanno vāyuḥ sarpagatiṃ dhatte ||
children.translated_text: But the recognition of the aggravated doṣa is not made from the gait named after a single creature; therefore the movements of two or three creatures have been shown. Thus deranged wind assumes the gait of a snake.

children.text: sāmyaṃ gato vāyuḥ jalaukāgatiṃ dhatte evamanye'pi jñeyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Wind that has reached equilibrium assumes the gait of a leech. The others too should be understood in the same way.
When two doṣas are aggravated, it should be known as sometimes moving slowly and sometimes flowing swiftly.
When it has shifted from its proper place, it kills.

children.text: yā dhamanī sthitvā sthitvā calati sā prāṇanāśinī smṛtā kathitā ||
children.translated_text: The artery that moves after pausing again and again is remembered, that is, described, as destructive of life.

children.text: atikṣīṇā śītā gacchatī satī prāṇino jīvitaṃ jīvanāśam asaṃśayaṃ niḥsaṃdehena hanti dūrīkarotītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When it moves as extremely weak and cold, it certainly, without doubt, destroys, that is, removes, the life of a living being.
Now, the purification of metals.

children.text: svarṇādayaḥ ete sapta dhātavo vijñeyāstān budhaḥ taddoṣaniḥsāraṇārthaṃ śodhayet ||
children.translated_text: Gold and the rest are to be known as these seven metals; a wise person should purify them in order to remove their defects.

children.text: tāraḥ raupyam iti pittalo nāgaḥ sīsakaḥ sīsakaṃ tīkṣṇaloham ||
children.translated_text: Tāra means silver; pittala is brass; nāga is lead; sīsaka is lead; and tīkṣṇa-loha is iron.
Now, the purification of metals.

children.text: svarṇādidhātūnāṃ patrāṇi tailādau tridhā trivāram agnau pratāpayet taptvā taptvā niṣiñcayet nirvāpayet ||
children.translated_text: One should heat the leaves of gold and the other metals in fire three times, or three rounds, in oil and the like, and after heating them again and again one should pour them in, that is, quench them.
In this way the purification of gold and the other metals is fully produced.

children.text: nāgavaṅgayor viśeṣeṇa śodhanamāha tadā viśuddhiḥ syāt ||
children.translated_text: He states the special purification of lead and tin: then there will be complete purity.

children.text: nanu pittalaḥ kṛtrimastatkathaṃ sapta ucyante eke yaśadena saha sapta āhuḥ ||
children.translated_text: Objection: brass is artificial, so how are seven metals spoken of? Some say there are seven together with zinc.

children.text: tathā ca svarṇaṃ rūpyaṃ ca tāmraṃ ca raṅgaṃ yaśadameva ca
children.translated_text: Thus: gold, silver, copper, tin, and zinc as well,

children.text: sīsaṃ lohaṃ ca saptaite dhātavo girisambhavāḥ
children.translated_text: lead and iron: these seven metals are mountain-born.
So it is said.

children.text: atha svarṇādidhātumāraṇaṃ tatrādau śārṅgadharānuktamapi svarṇotpattibhedaśuddhāśuddhalakṣaṇamāha athotpattiḥ
children.translated_text: Now the incineration of gold and the other metals. There, at the beginning, although it is not stated by <s>Śārṅgadhara</s>, he describes the origin, varieties, and marks of pure and impure gold. Now, its origin:
In ancient times, when the seven seers, self-controlled, were dwelling in their own hermitages,
the wives, endowed with beauty, prosperity, and youth, were seen,
and the mind of <s>Jātavedas</s>, shattered by the pride of Love,
released seed that fell upon the surface of the earth and became gold.

children.text: atha bhedāḥ prākṛtaṃ sahajaṃ vahnisambhūtaṃ khanijaṃ tathā
children.translated_text: Now the varieties: natural, innate, fire-born, mineral, and likewise
that produced by the penetration of rasendra; gold is considered fivefold.

children.text: brahmāṇḍaṃ saṃvṛtaṃ yena durlabhaṃ prākṛtaṃ hi tat
children.translated_text: That by which the cosmic egg is enclosed is rare and is indeed natural gold.
The brahmavrata gold is innate, and the fire-born is proclaimed as produced from fire.
This triad of gold is divine; and that which is joined with inauspicious colors,
by merely wearing it, can make the body free from old age and death.
Mineral gold is born from mining, and penetrated gold from rasa-penetration.
Endowed with fourteen colors, when eaten it conquers every disease.
Now the examination of impure gold.

children.text: śvetāṅgaṃ kaṭhinaṃ rūkṣaṃ vivarṇaṃ ca samardalam
children.translated_text: Whitish in body, hard, rough, discolored, and with equal layers,

children.text: dāhe chede sitaṃ śvetaṃ gharṣe cāpi malaṃ tyajet ||
children.translated_text: in burning and cutting it is pale or white, and in rubbing it also gives off impurity.
This means when gold has been made into leaves like birch bark by hammering.

children.text: sūtaṃ śuddhaṃ hiṅgulotthaṃ vā dviguṇam amlena nimbukādirasena saha mardayet ||
children.translated_text: One should triturate purified mercury, or mercury derived from cinnabar, in double quantity together with an acid such as lemon juice.

children.text: tadgolakasamaṃ gandhakam adharottaraṃ dadyāt ūrdhvādhaḥ sa eva madhye mudrayitvā triṃśadvanopalaiḥ puṭet ||
children.translated_text: One should place sulfur equal to that pellet below and above; sealing that very thing in the middle, one should heat it with thirty forest-cow-dung cakes.
Thus, after fourteen heatings, it becomes non-revivable.
An equal amount of sulfur should be added at each heating.

children.text: kāñcane svarṇe gālite nāgaṃ sīsakaṃ ṣoḍaśāṃśena nikṣipet ||
children.translated_text: Into melted gold one should add lead in the amount of one sixteenth.

children.text: taccūrṇayitvā amlena ghṛṣṭvā golakaṃ kṛtvā samaṃ gandhakam ūrdhvādhaḥ śarāvasaṃpuṭe pūrvavat ||
children.translated_text: Having powdered that, rubbed it with acid, and made a pellet, one should place an equal amount of sulfur above and below in a covered pair of earthen saucers, as before.

children.text: anyacca kāñcanārarasaiḥ samasūtakagandhayoḥ kajjalī hemapatrāṇi lepayet ||
children.translated_text: And further: with the juices of kāñcanāra, one should smear gold leaves with a black paste of equal parts purified mercury and sulfur.
In an equal measure, in a measure equal to the gold; the rest is clear.
Another method for incinerating gold.

children.text: śilā manaḥśilā sindūraṃ tayoḥ samayos tulyayoś cūrṇam arkadugdhaṃ dadyāt ||
children.translated_text: Orpiment, realgar, and cinnabar: one should give the powder of these two, in equal amounts, with the milky sap of arka.

children.text: dhamettato hemni dugdhakaiḥ samaiva bhāgato dadyāt dhamettato hemni gālite samaḥ hemasamaḥ kalkaḥ dīyeta tato dhamet ||
children.translated_text: Then one should blow it in the fire upon the gold; with milky substances one should add it in an equal share to the melted gold, the paste being equal to the gold, and then blow it in the fire.

children.text: yathā kalko na tiṣṭhati evaṃ kṣāratrayaṃ dadyāt svarṇamṛtirbhavet ||
children.translated_text: In such a way that the paste does not remain, one should add the three alkalis; the ash of gold will result.
And likewise the passage beginning 'pārāvata' is easy to understand.
Another method, from another treatise.

children.text: daradaṃ hiṃgulaṃ svarṇatulyaṃ nāgaṃ sīsakaṃ mṛtaṃ nāgacūrṇaṃ vajrīkṣīreṇa marditam asya madhye suvarṇasya kalkaśca mriyate iti svarṇamāraṇam ||
children.translated_text: Darada, cinnabar, lead equal to the gold, dead lead, and powdered lead are triturated with the milk of vajrī; within this the paste of gold also is killed. Thus is the incineration of gold.
Now he states the origins and varieties of silver, from another treatise.
For the purpose of killing <s>Tripura</s>, with eyes that did not blink,
<s>Śiva</s>, filled with anger, gazed steadily.
Then, at the time of the fiery omen, from that particular eye,
<s>Rudra</s> arose from it, blazing like <s>Vaiśvānara</s> fire.
From the second, further eye there came ten drops, from the red areca-like one;
from that arose wondrous silver, established for auspicious rites.
Thus.

children.text: atha tadbhedāḥ sahajaṃ khanisambhūtaṃ kṛtrimaṃ ca tridhā matam ||
children.translated_text: Now its divisions: it is considered threefold, innate, mine-born, and artificial.
Silver, each earlier kind, by its own qualities, is superior to each later kind.
The artificial kind is produced from <s>rasavāda</s> (alchemy), or else is said to arise from <s>Rāma</s>'s foot.

children.text: niṣkalmaṣaṃ prabhāhīnaṃ dāhe chede sitaṃ śubham
children.translated_text: That which is stainless, without dullness of lustre, and white in burning and cutting, is pure and good.

children.text: aśuddhaṃ sarvathā śodhyaṃ nāgaṃ dattvā vicakṣaṇaiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Impure silver should by all means be purified by the skilled, after adding <s>nāga</s> (lead).
Thus.
Now the incineration, in one part.
The rest is clear.
And another method.

children.text: snuhīkṣīreṇa sehuṇḍadugdhena sampiṣṭamākṣikaṃ svarṇamākṣikaṃ mūtrādau śuddhaṃ tālakasya prakāreṇa bhāgaikatārapatrāṇi vibhāgaṃ vilepayet punaḥ mūṣāsaṃpuṭena ruddhvā caturdaśapuṭaiḥ puṭet ||
children.translated_text: Gold pyrites, purified in urine and the like, is ground with the milk of <s>snuhī</s> and the latex of <s>sehuṇḍa</s>; according to the method for orpiment, one should smear one-part silver leaves separately, seal them again in a crucible casing, and heat them with fourteen <s>puṭa</s> firings.
The silver becomes ash.

children.text: granthāntare pāradena māraṇaṃ kṛtaṃ tadapi likhyate tathā ca
children.translated_text: In another treatise an incineration by mercury is made; that too is written as follows.
Having made a paste with mercury, one should then mix it with silver.
Afterwards one should triturate equal parts of orpiment and sulphur with lemon juice.
With two or three <s>puṭa</s> firings it becomes ash; this should be employed in mercury preparations and the like.
Thus.
Now the properties.
Silver is cooling, astringent and sour, with a sweet post-digestive taste, and is laxative.
It sustains age, is unctuous, scraping, and conquers <s>vāta</s> and <s>pitta</s>.
It certainly destroys diseases such as <s>prameha</s> quickly.
Now the incineration of brass.

children.text: ārasya pītalohasya patrāṇi amladravair nimbukādyaiḥ śuddhe mūṣāpuṭe pacet ||
children.translated_text: Leaves of <s>āra</s>, yellow metal, should be cooked with sour liquids such as lemon in a purified crucible firing.

children.text: nirguṇḍikā tāmraṃ prasiddhaṃ rītiḥ pittaliḥ dhvaniḥ kāṃsyaṃ tadvadhe tanmāraṇe spaṣṭamanyat ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nirguṇḍikā</s>, copper, the well-known alloy, brass, sounding bronze, and bell-metal: for their killing, that is, their incineration, the rest is clear.
Now the origin, varieties, incineration, and properties of copper and the others.
The seed of <s>Kārttikeya</s> that fell upon the surface of the earth,
from that, the ancient knowers say, this copper arose.
Thus.
Now the varieties.
There are two coppers, Nepalese and foreign; in mercurial work, the Nepalese is best.
The foreign kind is whitish, dark-red in hue, and very inferior.
The Nepalese kind is very unctuous, soft, red, and free from alteration.

children.text: imaṃ rūkṣam atistabdhaṃ śvetaṃ vāpi ca vāsaham
children.translated_text: This other one is rough, very stiff, white, or else ill-smelling.
It is said to be mixed with iron and lead; having heard this, know the seven faults of it.

children.text: eko doṣo viṣe tāmre tvaṣṭau doṣāḥ prakīrtitāḥ
children.translated_text: In copper there is one fault as in poison; eight faults are declared.
Dizziness, fainting, burning, sweating, nausea, and vomiting,
loss of appetite and mental distress: when drunk, these faults are like poison.

children.text: viṣavatsthāpitaṃ tāmraṃ yatnataḥ sādhyate hi tat
children.translated_text: Copper, treated as if it were poison, is indeed to be prepared carefully.
Thus.
Now the incineration.
<s>Mīnākṣī</s>, <s>matsyagandhā</s>, and <s>cāṅgerī</s>; the rest is clear.
And another method: fine copper leaves, in a quantity of two palas,
should be steamed daily in cow urine for twenty-one days.
Then, having put them again into a sour liquid, one should keep them for seven days.
Having added mercury equal to one fourth part, and an equal amount of powdered salt-mixture,
one should put the leaves into a mortar and triturate all of that.
For a period of seven days, with sulphur equal to the whole,
having made it into black sulphide paste, one should apply it below and above on the leaves.
In a pot, after sealing it properly with a dish,
and then filling it with sand, one should cook it for two praharas.
When it has cooled of itself, one should take it out and consume two raktikās.
Together with clove and long pepper, it destroys phlegmatic diseases.
Copper removes dyspnea and cough, destroys <s>vāta</s>, and conquers weakness of digestion.
In extremely phlegmatic diseases one should drink <s>vāsā</s> and <s>kṣudrā</s> after it.
Thus, from another treatise, <s>Tāmreśvara</s>.

children.text: tāmraṃ kaṣāyaṃ madhuraṃ satiktamamlaṃ ca pāke kaṭu sārakaṃ ca
children.translated_text: Copper is astringent, sweet, somewhat bitter and sour, pungent in digestion, and laxative.

children.text: pittāpahaṃ śleṣmaharaṃ ca śītaṃ tadropaṇaṃ syāllaghulekhanaṃ vā ||
children.translated_text: It removes <s>pitta</s> and <s>śleṣman</s>, is cooling, and is either healing, light, and scraping.
Pallor, piles, fever, skin disease, cough, and wasting from injury,
when drunk, it treats all <s>pitta</s>, swelling, <s>kapha</s>, and colic.
Others say that this is slightly nourishing.
Thus the properties of copper.
Now the account of the origin and varieties of <s>nāga</s> (lead).
When <s>Vāsuki</s>, seeing a lovely serpent maiden, discharged
his semen, from that <s>nāga</s> was born, remover of all diseases for men.
It melts fluidly, is very heavy, black when cut, and bright.
It has a foul smell and is black outside; pure lead is otherwise.
Thus.
Now the incineration.

children.text: śilā manaḥśilā tāmbūlarasasampiṣṭanāgapatralepaḥ triṃśadbhiḥ puṭairbhogī nirutthaṃ bhasmatāṃ yāti ||
children.translated_text: A coating of lead leaves ground with realgar, <s>manaḥśilā</s>, and betel juice: by thirty <s>puṭa</s> firings, the serpent-metal becomes ash from which no metal revives.
And another method.

children.text: aśvatthaḥ pippalaḥ ciñcā amlikā tayos tvakcūrṇam ||
children.translated_text: <s>Aśvattha</s>, <s>pippala</s>, tamarind, and sour tamarind: the powder of their bark.
And another method.
By three <s>kumbhipuṭa</s> firings, lead triturated with the juice of <s>vāsā</s>,
together with realgar, becomes ash; that powder removes all diseases.
Thus, from another treatise.
With <s>kumbhapuṭa</s> and <s>gajapuṭa</s> firings, together with realgar, that is, with <s>manaḥśilā</s>.
Thus the incineration of lead.
Now tin.
Tin is said to be of two kinds, mixed and hoof-like.

children.text: khurakaṃ tu guṇaiḥ śreṣṭhaṃ miśrakaṃ na rase hitam ||
children.translated_text: But khuraka is superior in qualities; miśraka is not beneficial in rasa.
It is mobile, soft, unctuous, quick to melt, and heavy.
Khuravaṅga is noiseless; miśraka is dark and white.
Thus.
The rest is clear. Now the incineration.
Tin is burning in effect and cold; it conquers diseases caused by affliction of kapha,
the eighteen kinds of worms, and urinary disorders; there is no doubt about this.
Thus.

children.text: keciddāhaharaḥ śīta iti paṭhanti tatra madanavinodapathyāpathyanighaṇṭvādau vaṅgasyoṣṇaguṇasya likhitatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Some read, 'it removes burning and is cold'; but there, since in the <s>Madanavinoda</s>, <s>Pathyāpathyānighaṇṭu</s>, and other works the hot quality of tin is recorded,
and especially because, when killed with tāla, it is indeed hot.
From another treatise: <s>Vaṅgeśvara</s>.
One should melt purified mercury and purified tin and work them together.
Then one should triturate orpiment, equal to the two, with the liquid of śaṭhī.
When dry, one should cook it in a glass vessel for four yāmas.
Having added one fourth part of orpiment, one should cook it again three times.
One should take it in a dose of half a guñjā or one guñjā, according to strength.
It conquers vāta, kapha-type asthma, skin disease, cough, and fistula.
It also conquers vātarakta, wasting disease, weakness of digestive fire, and disorders of the three doṣas.
This mercury preparation, named <s>Vaṅgeśvara</s>, is honored in all diseases.
It is especially useful in vāta disorders such as paralysis and in conditions connected with childbirth.
Thus <s>Vaṅgeśvara</s>, from another treatise.
Now the purification, incineration, and adjuvants of tin are stated in particular.
First one should put it in cow's urine; second, one should put it in buttermilk.
Third, it should be put in sour gruel; fourth, in pungent oil.
The physician should carry out the purification under an auspicious ascendant and conjunction.
Tin that is melted and free from coating should be applied in all diseases.
Thus the purification of tin.
Now the incineration.
One should cook a vessel placed over a stove for two yāmas.

children.text: gharṣaṇaṃ lohadaṇḍena cūrṇaṃ deyaṃ punaḥ punaḥ ||
children.translated_text: It is to be rubbed with an iron rod, and powder should be added again and again.
First there is powder of turmeric, and second dīpyaka.
Third are the two kinds of cumin, and fourth tamarind bark.

children.text: evaṃ krameṇa cūrṇena vaṅgaṃ niścandrikaṃ bhavet
children.translated_text: With powders in this sequence, the tin becomes without metallic glitter.
When it has cooled of itself, one should take it out; the ash is white like the moon.
Well-prepared tin ash should be given in a dose of one guñjā.
I shall state the adjuvant, according to the adjuvant appropriate for each disease.
Joined with the fresh juice of dhātrī, it destroys obstinate urinary disease.
With the juice of śatāvarī, it removes painful urination.
With the juice of pāribhadra it removes excessive urination.
With turmeric powder, madhuka, and the juice of dhātrī fruit,
it destroys the four kinds of discharge; there is no doubt about this.
One should give it to drink with a decoction of the five bitter drugs; it conquers every skin disease.
Joined with sugar and honey, with the juice of kūṣmāṇḍa,
it destroys very obstinate bleeding disorder, wasting, cough, and asthma.
It should be drunk with the juice of kaṇṭakārī; it conquers the five kinds of cough.

children.text: mudgaṃ saśarkaraṃ kṣaudraṃ jāṅgalaṃ piśitaṃ rasam ||
children.translated_text: One should use mung beans with sugar and honey, and the meat-soup of wild animals,
as well as the fruit of uduṃbara, taṇḍulīyaka, and vāstuka,
plantain blossom, cāṅgerī, ayaka, and plantain fruit.
One should also use fresh butter and milk, and should perform oil massage and bathing.
Thus the section on preparations of tin.
Now the incineration of iron.

children.text: pātālagaruḍī pātālamūlī kuṭhāraḥ anyacca daradaṃ hiṃgulaṃ tīkṣṇagatavallīcūrṇam ||
children.translated_text: Pātālagaruḍī, pātālamūlī, kuṭhāra, and also darada, hiṅgula, and powder of tīkṣṇagatavallī.
And another method.
'With juices,' thus.
Another passage too is easy to understand.
Now the section on preparations of iron.

children.text: pātañjale tathā tantre lohā bahuvidhā matāḥ ||
children.translated_text: In the <s>Pātañjala</s> and likewise in the tantra, irons are considered to be of many kinds.
Because they are hard to obtain and fruitless, I write the divisions here.
Because of their excellence, bhadra and vajra, and such kinds as pāṇḍikānta,
are described according to their forms and qualities, from the region of <s>Nāgārjuna</s>.
Kali is said to be twice the common kind, and eight times beyond that.
Bhadra is ten times kali, and vajra is a thousandfold beyond bhadra.
Beyond vajra, multiplied a thousand times, pāḍinī is ten times greater.
Then, through a thousand crores, magnetic iron is greatly efficacious.
Thus.
There the specific distinction is stated.
That conquered by sour gruel and having the weight of a tulā is known as iron of the color of ghee.

children.text: kāśatāḍaṃ kṛśāṅgaṃ ca śulāṃ gandho dudeśatam ||
children.translated_text: Kāśatāḍa, thin-bodied, and śulā, with its smell, are described from that region.

children.text: paṇḍitaṃ dvividhaṃ kṛṣṇaṃ śuklaṃ ca samatārdrakam
children.translated_text: Paṇḍita is twofold, black and white, and equally moist.
Bhadra resembles castor seeds and likewise the leaf of snuhī.
Vajra resembles a damana leaf and has a slight golden lustre.
Kānta is very soft; tāra-rukma-kānta has a white-making appearance.
Where paste of nimba, left day and night, becomes sweet,
that is the best kānta; and that which occurs in the form of stone is vārttika.
Kahvoṇa is the best magnetic iron; anything other than that is considered middling.
Kṣudrāṇḍa and gurutāḍa are considered to be iron born in Kaliṅga.
Shining like gold and non-gold, sharp and with soft effect, it is considered so.
Born from each particular mine, it removes each corresponding disease.
Therefore, in the examination of it, one proceeds to that particular test, though the wording is uncertain.
Thus the kinds of iron.
Now the incineration.

children.text: vajraṃ pañcādikaṃ teṣāṃ bhedā yājyatamaṃ śubham
children.translated_text: Among these, vajra and the five and more varieties are the most suitable and auspicious.

children.text: prākpañcapalād ūrdhvaṃ yāvad ā ṣoḍaśaṃ palam ||
children.translated_text: From more than five palas up to sixteen palas.
Now the purification of iron.
With water three times the amount of triphalā; triphalā is sixteen palas.
But when one quarter remains of that decoction, one should make five palas of iron into leaves, heat them, and quench them seven times.
Having made leaves and heated them, one should quench them seven times.
In this way the mountain-born defect produced in iron is dissolved.
Thus.
Now, praise of the heating cycle in incineration.
Through heating cycles there is destruction of defects; from the heating cycle alone the arising of virtues occurs.
And iron is killed by a heating cycle; therefore one should perform heating cycles.
As many and more heating cycles as are applied to iron,
so, correspondingly, its virtues increase by hundreds and thousands.
The physician should heat the iron in cycles until, when powdered in water,
because of its lightness it floats upon the water like a goose.
Nor should he stop grinding it in this way until it resembles collyrium,

children.text: karoti nihitaṃ netre naiva pīḍā manāgapi ||
children.translated_text: and, when placed in the eye, it causes not even the slightest pain.
At each heating cycle, after decocting it, he should give a pot-cooking process.
Or, through fear of expense, washing may be done after every single heating cycle.
Thus.
Now he states the heating cycles according to the division of doṣas.

children.text: pākaḥ phalāmbudaśamūlarasena vāyau pitte tu śītamadhurais triphalairvidāryāḥ
children.translated_text: For vāyu the cooking is with the juice of phalāmbu and daśamūla; but for pitta it is with cooling and sweet substances, with triphalā and vidārī.

children.text: tajjñaiḥ śatāvarijaṭāsvarasena deyaḥ śleṣmāṇake tu daśamūlarasārdrakeṇa ||
children.translated_text: By those who know, it should be given with the fresh juice of the root of <s>śatāvarī</s>; but in a phlegmatic condition, with the juice of daśamūla and fresh ginger.
In disorders of vāta and śleṣman, and in swellings of various kinds,
especially with <s>varṣābhū</s> and <s>śṛṅgavera</s>, and with <s>māṇaka</s>.
Thus.
<s>Māṇaka</s> means <s>māṇakanda</s>.
In pitta and wind, and in blood combined with pitta, with grapes, vidārī, and śatamūlikā,
and with kṣīrakākolī and kākolī, with madhūka flowers, and also with dates,
they are to be given in just the same way.
Now he states the heating cycles according to the division of diseases.

children.text: jīrṇajvare guḍūcī kāse śvāse ca śasyate vyāghrī
children.translated_text: In chronic fever, guḍūcī is recommended; in cough and asthma, vyāghrī is praised.
For consumption, blood disease, and pitta disorders, vāsā is praised, and the plant named balā.
For the appeasement of nasal wounds and bleeding, the fresh juice of barley and dūrvā is used.
Water from the bark of kaṅkelli is praised in all cases of pradaras.
In pravāhikā, water produced from nicula leaves is especially praised.
In grahaṇī disorders, the decoction of mustaka is praised; in diarrheas, kuṭaja decoction.
In urinary disease, whether mild or severe, and in dysuria, pāṣāṇabhedikā and ativana are used.
The decoction of varṣābhū and nāgara is for the pacification of swelling.
Cow urine is praised in three conditions: abdominal disease, epilepsy, and pallor disease.
In wounds, māṇakanda is used; in abdominal tumors, rohītaka decoction.
In hiccup and asthma, the fresh juice of brāhmī and bhārgī is also praised.
The decoction of castor and nāgara is especially praised in a condition with āma.
In colics, it should be given with daśamūla, with cow urine, and with the water of phala.
In diseases of the liver and spleen, the milk of gṛhakanyā and arka should be given.
In worms it is considered proper with devadāru, viḍaṅga, and palāśa.
In skin disease, with sampāka, nimba, saptaparṇa, and aṭarūṣaka.
With bhallātaka, vākucī, vṛndārka, and aśana,
and with sweet preparations of sugarcane juice, with abhīrū and varuṇa as well.
With the roots of the five castor-grasses and with śailūṣaka,
and with triphalā, it should be done in obstruction at the root, when it is due to all three doṣas.
In all cases of stones, and especially in retention of urine,
with the milky sap of trees, amṛtā, grapes, abhīrū, and daśamūla,
with these along with vājigandhā, it is prescribed also in wasting diseases.
In acid dyspepsia, heating cycles should everywhere be given with śatāvarī.
Muṇḍikā, śatamūlī, and with citrāṅga, karikarṇa, and keśarāja,

children.text: madhukaguḍūcīmārkavamusalībhallātakaiḥ kalpe rasāyane nāgabalā hayagandhā gokarṇakavṛddhadārakāmalakī vājīkaraṇe vihitā vānarīśatamūlikā kṣurikā jñātvaivam ||
children.translated_text: with madhuka, guḍūcī, mārkava, musalī, and bhallātaka in a rasāyana preparation; and nāgabalā, hayagandhā, gokarṇaka, vṛddhadāraka, and āmalakī are prescribed for virilization, with vānarī, śatamūlikā, and kṣurikā. One should know this.

children.text: rogaviśeṣānebhirvāratrayaṃ puṭena sthālīpāke adhikataḥ puruṣasvabhāvaṃ buddhimānkathitamapi hemamauṣadham ucitam upādeyam anyadapi ||
children.translated_text: Having understood the particular diseases, with these substances, three times by the heating cycle, or more by pot-cooking according to a person's constitution, the wise person should take up the gold medicine that has been stated as suitable, and also any other suitable medicine.

children.text: yaḥ kalpakāmaḥ kurute ca lohaṃ sa sarvaśaṅkāparivarjitāṅgaḥ
children.translated_text: He who, desiring the rejuvenating regimen, prepares iron, his body free from every doubt,
would always live on earth like an immortal, having the form of a person twice eight years old.
Thus.
The regimen of iron is complete.
Now, dross.
Heated in a decoction of cow urine and triphalā, it is to be purified twenty-one times.
This brings about the virtues of the dross of all metals, beginning with gold.
Thus, the incineration of dross from iron and the other metals.
Now, the measure for consuming metals beginning with gold.
Gold should be administered in the amount of two barley grains, up to the limit of eight guñjās.
Silver is twice that; iron and the others are three times that amount.
Now, the purification and incineration of secondary minerals.

children.text: mākṣikaṃ svarṇamākṣikaṃ tutthaṃ tutthakam abhram abhrakaṃ nīlāñjanaṃ kṛṣṇāñjanam manaḥśilā ālakaḥ haritālakaḥ rasakaḥ kharparam ||
children.translated_text: Mākṣika is svarṇamākṣika; tuttha is tutthaka; abhra is abhraka; nīlāñjana is black collyrium; manaḥśilā, ālaka, haritālaka, rasaka, and kharpara.
These are to be known as the seven secondary minerals.

children.text: yāvat pātraṃ lohitaṃ raktaṃ bhavati tāvat pacet ||
children.translated_text: One should cook it until the vessel becomes red, that is, blood-colored.
Then mākṣika reaches purification, that is, obtains purity.
The usage is due to substitution by ṛcchādeśa for the root ṛ, 'to go'.
Mākṣika is formed with a kṛt suffix and is neuter in gender.
Now, incineration.
The phrase beginning 'of kulattha' is clear; the rest is also clear.
Now, the purification and incineration of tāramākṣika.
Karkoṭī, namely barren karkoṭī, and meṣaśṛṅgī are well known.
Now, the incineration is as in the case of svarṇamākṣika.
Now, the purification of tuttha, with the phrase 'with dung'.
And in another treatise the purification is as follows:

children.text: ataḥ viṣṭhāsamaṃ tutthaṃ sakṣaudraṃ ṭaṃkaṇaṃ kṛtam
children.translated_text: Therefore tuttha equal to dung, together with honey, is made into ṭaṅkaṇa.
Purified by being heated in a closed crucible three times, it is free from vomiting and dizziness.
This is called black mica.
Objection: in another treatise mica is stated to be fourfold, as follows:

children.text: pinākaṃ darduraṃ nāgaṃ vajraṃ ceti caturvidham
children.translated_text: Pināka, dardura, nāga, and vajra: it is fourfold.

children.text: tat puṃnapuṃsakaṃ jñeyaṃ pratyekaṃ tatra lakṣaṇaiḥ ||
children.translated_text: It should be known as male and neuter, respectively, by their marks.
<s>Vaṅgasena</s> and others say that it is threefold:

children.text: vajraṃ bhekavapuḥ kṛṣṇābhrakaṃ ca trividhaṃ matam
children.translated_text: Vajra, frog-bodied, and black mica: it is considered threefold.
Then, taking the black one, one should cook it in good sour gruel.
So it is said.
<s>Trivikrama</s> explains this:

children.text: tataḥ kṛṣṇaṃ samādāyetyanena kṛṣṇatvasāmyād vajrakṛṣṇābhrayor grahaṇam ||
children.translated_text: By the phrase, "then, taking the black one," both vajra and black mica are included, because of their common blackness.
The frog-bodied kind, green, yellow, and other colors, is to be rejected.
Therefore <s>Śārṅgadhara</s> has taken only the black kind.
Now another method.
In the puṭa, that is, in the covered vessel, three puṭas should be given.
Balā is well known.
The rest is clear.
Thus ends the incineration of mica.
Now the purification of red ochre, green vitriol, borax, cowrie, conch, and torī is easy.
This means: in the same way as in the procedure for nīlāñjana, with impregnation in lemon juice.

children.text: gairikaṃ prasiddhaṃ kāsīsaṃ prasiddhaṃ ṭaṅkaṇaṃ kṣāraḥ varāṭikā śaṅkhaṃ torī sphaṭikā kaṅkuṣṭhaṃ cokaniryāsaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Gairika is well known; kāsīsa is well known; ṭaṅkaṇa is an alkali; varāṭikā is cowrie; śaṅkha is conch; torī is alum; kaṅkuṣṭha is the exudation of coka.
"One should cook it for three days" means this.
Others say as follows:
Realgar, ground with the juice of jayantī, is purified by heat.

children.text: viṣaghnī ca tridoṣaghnī sā śuddhā parikīrtitā ||
children.translated_text: When purified, it is declared to counteract poison and to remove the three doṣas.
One should put orpiment, piece by piece and fragment by fragment, that is, powdered orpiment, into sour gruel mixed with kali powder.

children.text: dolāpātre yāmaṃ pacet haṇḍikāyāṃ kāṣṭhaṃ dattvā kāṣṭhe lambamānāṃ poṭṭalikāṃ sthāpayet ||
children.translated_text: One should cook it for a yāma in a swing-vessel; placing a piece of wood in a pot, one should set the small bundle hanging from the wood.
This is the dolāyantra.
The rest is clear.
Rasaka is kharpara.
Now, the extraction of essence.

children.text: dhamanadravyāt lākṣādayaḥ pratyekamaṣṭamāṃśāḥ ṭaṅkaṇaṃ caturthāṃśamiti granthāntarāt ||
children.translated_text: From another treatise it is known that, among the blowing substances, lac and the rest are each one eighth, and borax is one fourth.
For, according to etymology, metals are so called from being blown.
The substances whose essence is to be extracted, such as mica and the rest, mean substances such as lead, copper, and so on.
Mīna means small fish.
Yavatiktā is sarpākṣī.
Or else yava is the well-known barley.
Tiktā is kaṭukī.

children.text: athetyanantaraṃ śārṅgadharānuktamapi ratnasaṃkhyām āha tatra pañca navaratnāni bhavanti tānyāha
children.translated_text: Now, after the word "atha," although not stated by <s>Śārṅgadhara</s>, he gives the number of jewels. There are five chief jewels and nine jewels; he states them:
There are five principal jewels and a group of four secondary jewels:

children.text: vajraṃ muktāphalaṃ caiva pravālaṃ mārkataṃ tathā ||
children.translated_text: diamond, pearl, coral, emerald, and likewise
topaz, sapphire, gomeda, and cat's-eye.
These are the nine jewels; a physician should purify and incinerate them.
So it is said.

children.text: vajraṃ hīrakaṃ pravālaṃ vidrumaṃ marakataḥ taddharitavarṇaṃ puṣparāgaṃ campakahemavarṇābhaṃ nīlam indranīlaṃ nīlavarṇaṃ vaiḍūryakaṃ vaidūryamaṇirbiḍālanetravarṇaṃ nīlapītavarṇam ||
children.translated_text: Vajra is diamond; pravāla is coral; marakata is emerald, green in color; puṣparāga resembles the color of campaka and gold; nīla is sapphire, blue in color; vaiḍūryaka is the vaidūrya gem, the color of a cat's eye, blue and yellow in color.

children.text: atha vajraśodhanaṃ vyāghrīkandaṃ guharīkandam iti śodhanam ||
children.translated_text: Now the purification of diamond: vyāghrīkanda and guharīkanda are the purifying agents.
Now the incineration.
Khara means donkey.
Matkuṇa means khaṭvamalla.
Another item too is hiṅgu and so forth.
The rest is also easy.
Now, the incineration of vaikrānta.
Vaikrānta is a diamond that has undergone alteration, a particular kind belonging to the class of diamonds.
The ancient jewel-examiners say "kapha" in this context.
Meṣadugdhī is well known.
Now the purification and incineration of the remaining jewels.
One should steam rubies and the like in a dolāyantra with the fresh juice of jayantī.
Maṇi means a gem such as sun-stone or moon-stone.
Or else, maṇi means the following gem.
And accordingly:

children.text: bhramaraśikhikaṇṭhavarṇaśikhāsamaprabho bhujaṅgānāṃ bhavati maṇiḥ kila mūrdhapriyo'narghyaguṇaḥ sa vijñeyaḥ
children.translated_text: The gem of serpents, colored like a bee and a peacock's throat and equal in brilliance to a crest, is said to be dear upon their heads; it should be known as having priceless qualities.
So it is said.
Pravāla is coral.

children.text: atha māraṇaṃ taṇḍulīyakaḥ meghanādaḥ śākaḥ stanyena strīdugdhena uktamākṣikavat svarṇamākṣikavat māraṇaṃ jambīrarasādau ||
children.translated_text: Now incineration: taṇḍulīyaka is meghanāda, a vegetable; stanya means woman's milk. Its incineration is as stated for mākṣika, that is, like gold-pyrites, in lemon juice and the like.
Now the purification of śilājatu.

children.text: grīṣme grīṣmakāle taptaśilācyutaṃ śilājatu samānīya yathā bhūmau na patati godugdhādibhirmardayet śudhyatīti ||
children.translated_text: In summer, that is, in the hot season, one should collect śilājatu that has flowed from heated rock and, so that it does not fall on the ground, triturate it with cow's milk and the like; thus it is purified.
Now the purification of that which has fallen on the ground is the principal procedure.

children.text: uttamaśilājatupāṣāṇaṃ sūkṣmakhaṇḍaprakalpitaṃ kṛtam atyuṣṇapānīye nikṣipya yāmaikaṃ sthāpayet ||
children.translated_text: Excellent śilājatu stone, made into small pieces, should be put into very hot water and left for one yāma.

children.text: mardayitvā tannīraṃ vastragālitaṃ gṛhṇīyāt mṛtpātre sthāpayitvā ātape dhārayet ||
children.translated_text: After triturating it, one should take that water filtered through cloth, place it in an earthen vessel, and keep it in the sun.
In another treatise, extraction in an iron vessel is stated.
For it is said, "four vessels of black iron."

children.text: uparisthe yat ghanaṃ tat anyapātre kṣipet ||
children.translated_text: Whatever thick substance is on top should be put into another vessel.

children.text: tatra jalaṃ dattvā tasmādanyasmin evaṃ dvimāsābhyāṃ jyeṣṭhāṣāḍhābhyāṃ niḥsārayet tato vahnikṣiptau liṅgopamaṃ liṅgākāraṃ bhavet tadā kāryakṣamaṃ kāryasādhakaṃ bhūyāditi parīkṣā ||
children.translated_text: Having added water there, one should transfer it from that into another vessel; in this way, during the two months <s>Jyeṣṭha</s> and <s>Āṣāḍha</s>, one should extract it. Then, when it is thrown into fire and becomes like a liṅga, that is, liṅga-shaped, then the test is that it becomes fit for use, capable of accomplishing the intended operation.
The rest is clear.
With embers, namely embers of vibhītaka, and with a decoction of triphalā, the amount is twice that of maṇḍūra.
Now, the preparation of alkali.
The woods of milky trees, such as apāmārga, tamarind, plantain, palāśa, sehuṇḍa, citraka, śigru, kaṇṭakārī, and others, are used.

children.text: pradīpayet jvālayet acchaṃ nirmalaṃ jalaṃ lohapātre kvāthayet ||
children.translated_text: One should kindle it, set it blazing; clear, pure water should be decocted in an iron vessel.

children.text: yastu cūrṇābhaḥ kṣāraḥ sa pratisāryaḥ maśakādau prayojyaḥ yastu kvāthavat dravarūpaḥ sthitaḥ sa gulmādau peyaḥ ityuktaṃ kṣāradvayam ||
children.translated_text: But the alkali that has the appearance of powder is for rubbing on, to be applied in cases such as mosquito bites; the one that remains in liquid form like a decoction is to be drunk in cases such as <s>gulma</s>. Thus the two kinds of alkali have been stated.
The powdered form should be administered in appropriate cases, such as <s>gulma</s>.
And likewise <s>Vāgbhaṭa</s> says:
Alkali is to be drunk in weakness of digestive fire, stone, <s>gulma</s>, abdominal disease, old age, and the like;
with alkali it is to be employed in months, in <s>citra</s>, external piles, skin disease, and numbness.
Now, the preparation of rasa.
<s>Pārada</s> (mercury) is the conqueror of all diseases, fever and the rest.
Likewise it is remembered as nourishing.

children.text: sujñena tatsādhakena sādhitaḥ tadā dehalohayoḥ siddhaṃ kuryāt ||
children.translated_text: When prepared by a skilled practitioner who accomplishes it, then it brings perfection to the body and to metals.

children.text: atha pāradanāmānyāha rasendraḥ rasānāmindra adhyakṣaḥ rasendraḥ pāradaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Now he states the names of <s>pārada</s>: <s>rasendra</s>, because it is the lord, the overseer, of the rasas; <s>rasendra</s> means <s>pārada</s>.
Because it gives passage across the ocean of diseases and the like, it is called <s>pārada</s>, and <s>sūta</s>.
Because it gives birth to the perfection of gold and the like, it is <s>sūta</s>.
<s>Haraja</s>: because it is born from <s>Hara</s>, it is <s>haraja</s>.

children.text: sūtakaḥ sūta eva sūtakaḥ svārthe kaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Sūtaka</s>: it is just <s>sūta</s>; the suffix -ka is in its own sense.
It is <s>rasa</s> because it is tasted and savored, since it possesses the six tastes.
<s>Mukunda</s>: it is <s>mukunda</s> because it gives <s>mukti</s>, liberation.
This follows from the Uṇādi derivation.
Now he states, in an easily understood way, the presiding deities of metals such as copper and of the sun and the others.

children.text: āraḥ pittaliḥ nāgaḥ sīsakaḥ hema svarṇaṃ vaṅgaṃ raṅgaṃ tīkṣṇaṃ tīkṣṇalohaṃ kāntalohaṃ vṛttaloham ||
children.translated_text: <s>Āra</s> is brass; <s>nāga</s> is lead; <s>sīsaka</s> is lead; <s>hema</s> is gold; <s>vaṅga</s> is tin; <s>raṅga</s> is tin; <s>tīkṣṇa</s> is sharp iron; magnetic iron and round iron are kinds of iron.
Now, the purification of mercury.

children.text: rājikā rasono lasunaḥ etayor mūṣāyāṃ rasaṃ pāradaṃ vibandhayet ||
children.translated_text: <s>Rājikā</s> is mustard, and <s>rasona</s> is garlic; with these two, one should confine rasa, that is <s>pārada</s>, in a crucible.
This is steaming.
Now, trituration.
One should triturate it for one day in a mortar; so it is said.
<s>Kākamācī</s> is well known.
Now, by other means there is trituration, stupefaction, or upward sublimation.
Now, the extraction of mercury from <s>darada</s>.

children.text: daradaṃ hiṅgulaḥ daradam ūrdhvaṃ pātayet ḍamaruyantre sūtavat ||
children.translated_text: <s>Darada</s> is cinnabar. One should sublime <s>darada</s> upward in a <s>ḍamaruyantra</s>, as in the case of <s>sūta</s>.
The rest is clear.

children.text: amī kālakūṭādayo nava viṣabhedāḥ prakīrtitāḥ kathitāḥ ||
children.translated_text: These nine varieties of poison, beginning with <s>kālakūṭa</s>, are proclaimed, that is, stated.
Their characteristics are to be learned from the examiners of poisons.

children.text: atha upaviṣāṇyāha lāṅgalī kalihārī karavīrakaḥ aśvamārajaṭārasaḥ ahiphenam āphūkam etāḥ sapta upaviṣajātayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Now he states the subsidiary poisons: <s>lāṅgalī</s>, <s>kalihārī</s>, <s>karavīraka</s>, the juice of the root of <s>aśvamāra</s>, <s>ahiphena</s>, and <s>āphūka</s>; these are the seven classes of subsidiary poison.

children.text: etairmarditaḥ sūtaḥ chinnapakṣaḥ jāyate mukhaṃ dhātugrasanaśīlam ato dhātūn tvarayā grasate ||
children.translated_text: Mercury triturated with these becomes one whose wings are cut; it obtains a mouth, that is, a capacity for devouring metals, and therefore it quickly consumes metals.

children.text: kālakūṭādīnāṃ dravaiḥ sapta sapta dinaṃ mardanaṃ prakṣālanaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: With the liquids of <s>kālakūṭa</s> and the others, trituration and washing are done for seven days each.
There is also another way of making the mouth.

children.text: kṣāraḥ svarjīyavakṣārau rājī rājikā rasonaṃ laśunaṃ navasāro navasāgaraḥ śigruḥ śobhāñjanam ||
children.translated_text: The alkalis are <s>svarjī-kṣāra</s> and <s>yava-kṣāra</s>; <s>rājī</s> is <s>rājikā</s>; <s>rasona</s> is garlic; <s>navasāra</s> is <s>navasāgara</s>; <s>śigru</s> is <s>śobhāñjana</s>.
<s>Dhātucara</s> means possessing the quality of devouring metals.
And another procedure:

children.text: bindulīkīṭaiḥ kīṭaviśeṣaiḥ lavaṇaṃ saindhavam amlairnimbukādyaiḥ dhātughasmaraṃ dhātubhakṣakaṃ mukhaṃ jāyate ||
children.translated_text: With <s>bindulī</s> insects, particular insects, with salt, namely rock salt, and with sour substances such as lemon, a metal-devouring mouth, one that eats metals, is produced.
Now the digestion of sulfur by means of the tortoise apparatus is stated.

children.text: tatrādau kacchapayantramāha atheti mṛtkuṇḍe nīraṃ nikṣipet tanmadhye mṛtkuṇḍapidhānaṃ śarāvakaṃ sthāpayet ||
children.translated_text: There, first, he describes the tortoise apparatus. After the word 'now': one should place water in an earthen pot, and in the middle of it set an earthen-pot lid, a small bowl.

children.text: kiṃbhūtaṃ madhyaṃ mekhalayā yutaṃ tryaṅgulonnatā mṛdracitā mekhalā madhyaṃ cūrṇena lepayet ||
children.translated_text: What is the middle like? It is furnished with a girdle: a clay-made girdle three fingers high. One should smear the middle with powder.

children.text: tanmadhye pāradaṃ dattvā tulyagandhakacūrṇaṃ dattvā upari śarāvaṃ dattvā bhasmalavaṇamudrāḥ kāryāścaturbhir utpalaiḥ puṭet ||
children.translated_text: Having put mercury in the middle, and having added an equal amount of sulfur powder, one should put a bowl over it, make seals of ash and salt, and heat it with four cow-dung cakes.
In this way it digests six times the amount of sulfur.
Poison too should be added along with the sulfur.

children.text: atra svarṇajāraṇaṃ noktaṃ granthāntarāllikhyate abījajīrṇasya māritasya doṣarūpatvāt
children.translated_text: Here the digestion of gold has not been stated; it is written from another treatise, because mercury killed without the seed being digested has the nature of a fault.
And accordingly:

children.text: ajīrṇaṃ śambhubījaṃ tu sūtakaṃ yastu jārayet
children.translated_text: Whoever digests undigested <s>Śambhu</s>'s seed, namely mercury,

children.text: brahmahā sa durācārī mama drohī maheśvari ||
children.translated_text: that evil-behaved man is a slayer of a Brahmin and hostile to me, O <s>Maheśvarī</s>.
Now, the digestion:
A gold leaf measuring one sixty-fourth part, with peacock bile,
smeared and placed in a heated mortar: after adding mercury, one should triturate it.
Again with lemon water, for each morsel this same procedure is to be followed.
One should gently steam it again, after binding it in a closed vessel with sour gruel.

children.text: bhāṇḍike tridinaṃ sthāpya sūtaṃ jīrṇaṃ samuddharet
children.translated_text: Having kept it for three days in a vessel, one should take out the mercury when it has been digested.
If, when weighed, it is greater, then it should again be steamed for the same length of time.
The digestion of the metal is, in sequence, with a thirty-second, a sixteenth, and an eighth part.

children.text: rūpyādiṣu ca sattveṣu vidhirevaṃ paraṃ smṛtaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In silver and other essences too, this very method is remembered as the supreme one.
With <s>māyūramāyu</s>, that is, with peacock bile, the gold leaf is excellent gold.

children.text: dhūmasāram aṅgāradhūmaṃ śuddhaṃ pāradaṃ torī gurjaradeśodbhavā sphaṭikā yā raktavarṇā bhavati ||
children.translated_text: <s>Dhūmasāra</s> is charcoal smoke; purified mercury; <s>torī</s> is a crystal born in the Gurjara country, which is red in color.
Sulfur is purified; <s>navasādara</s> is <s>navasāgara</s>.
All this is in equal quantity.
The rest is clear.
And likewise another procedure:

children.text: apāmārga ūrdhvakaṇṭakaḥ malayūdugdhaṃ kāṣṭhodumbarikādugdhaṃ droṇapuṣpī prasiddhā tatpuṣpāṇi viḍaṅgam irimedo viṭkhadiraḥ cūrṇam etaccūrṇam ūrdhvordhvaṃ dīyate spaṣṭamanyat ||
children.translated_text: <s>Apāmārga</s> is <s>ūrdhvakaṇṭaka</s>; <s>malayūdugdha</s> is the milk of the woody fig; <s>droṇapuṣpī</s> is well known. Its flowers, <s>viḍaṅga</s>, <s>irimeda</s>, <s>viṭkhadira</s>, and the powder: this powder is added successively again and again. The rest is clear.
And another procedure:
<s>Kāṣṭhodumbarikā</s> is well known.
And another procedure:
The meaning of <s>nāgavallī</s> is clear.
<s>Jvālāmukhī</s> is well known.

children.text: pāradaṃ śuddhaṃ rasakaṃ kharparaṃ tālaṃ tutthaṃ śuddhaṃ ṭaṅkaṇaṃ saubhāgyakṣāraṃ kāravellī śākaviśeṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Purified mercury, rasaka, kharpara, orpiment, purified tuttha, borax, saubhāgya alkali, and kāravellī, a particular kind of vegetable.
A copper vessel is purified in cow urine, pañcāmṛta, and the like.
The rest is clear.
The wholesome diet is milk-rice, or mudga beans.

children.text: tāmraṃ mṛtaṃ vajrī sehuṇḍabhedaḥ dantī jayapālamūlaṃ trivṛnniśothaḥ māṣamātraṃ siddhaṃ rasaṃ pañcāśanmaricaṃ guḍaṃ gadyāṇakaṃ ṣaṇmāṣakaṃ tulasīdalapalaṃ dvayaṃ dvigadyāṇakam etatpramāṇaṃ tridinaṃ kṛtvā bhakṣayet ||
children.translated_text: Incinerated copper; vajrī, a type of sehuṇḍa; dantī; the root of jayapāla; trivṛt, that is niśotha; one māṣa of the perfected rasa; fifty peppers; one gadyāṇaka of jaggery, six māṣakas; and two palas of tulasī leaves, that is two gadyāṇakas: having prepared this measure, one should eat it for three days.
Or else for seven days, because of the abundance of the medicine.

children.text: rasāt pāradāt śuddhāt bhāgaikaḥ elīyaḥ elavālukaṃ pippalī śivā harītakī ākārakarabhaḥ ākallakaḥ gandho gandhakaḥ kaṭutailena drāvayitvā śodhitaḥ indravāruṇyāḥ phalāni amī elīyādayaḥ caturbhāgāḥ pratyekaṃ punaḥ indravāruṇikārasaiḥ mardayet māṣamātrāṃ vaṭīṃ khādet ||
children.translated_text: From rasa, that is purified mercury, one part; elīya, that is elavāluka; pippalī; śivā, that is harītakī; ākārakarabha, that is ākallaka; gandha, that is sulfur, melted and purified with pungent oil; the fruits of indravāruṇī; these, beginning with elīya, are each four parts. Then one should triturate them with the juices of indravāruṇikā and eat a pill the size of a māṣa.
A dry powder should be made from indravāruṇikā fruit.

children.text: śuddhaḥ sūtaḥ pāradaḥ bhāgadvayamiti ṭaṅkadvayaṃ karṣadvayaṃ tathā gandhakasya śuddhasya dvau bhāgau tayoḥ pāradagandhakayoḥ kajjalikāṃ kuryāt ||
children.translated_text: Purified sūta, that is mercury, is two parts, meaning two ṭaṅkas or two karṣas; likewise two parts of purified sulfur. Of those two, mercury and sulfur, one should make kajjalī.

children.text: sūtāt caturguṇeṣu aṣṭabhāgeṣu kapardeṣu kṣipet bhāgaikaṃ ṭaṅkaṇaṃ saubhāgyaṃ dattvā gokṣīreṇa mardayitvā varāṭānāṃ mukhaṃ mudrayet śaṃkhasya śaṃkhānām aṣṭau bhāgān śarāvamadhye varāṭakānām adha ūrdhvaṃ dattvā mudrāṃ vidhāya gajapuṭe pacet kapardo varāṭakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Into kapardas amounting to four times the sūta, that is eight parts, one should put one part of ṭaṅkaṇa, namely saubhāgya, triturate with cow’s milk, and seal the mouths of the varāṭas. Having placed eight parts of śaṅkha shells below and above the varāṭakas inside a saucer, sealed it, one should cook it in a gajapuṭa. Kaparda means varāṭaka.

children.text: puṭasyāntaḥ saṃpuṭasyāntaḥ sarvaṃ kṣipet cūrṇaṃ kajjalīcūrṇaṃ talliptaśarāvayoḥ saṃpuṭasyāntaḥ madhye ṣaḍguñjāsaṃmite rasaṃ siddham ekonatriṃśat ūṣaṇairmaricairdeyaṃ vātaroge ghṛtena dadyāt ||
children.translated_text: Inside the puṭa, that is inside the sealed container, one should put everything: the powder, the kajjalī powder, inside the enclosure of the two saucers smeared with it. In the middle, the perfected rasa, measuring six guñjās, should be given with twenty-nine pungent peppers; in disease of vāta it should be given with ghee.
Śapharī is a small fish.
For it has been included in the class of wholesome foods.
Because <s>Suśruta</s> says, "Rohita is the best among fishes."

children.text: ayuktanidrāṃ divājanyā jayā vijayā taccūrṇaṃ kolamajjāṃ badaramajjāṃ kaṇā pippalī barhirmayūrastatpakṣabhasma ||
children.translated_text: Irregular sleep is sleep produced by day; jayā and vijayā are its powder; kolamajjā means the pith of badara; kaṇā is pippalī; barhi is the peacock, and that is the ash of its feathers.

children.text: bhūrjapatravat tanu sūkṣmaṃ yathā syāttathā hemnaḥ suvarṇasya patrāṇi kārayet ||
children.translated_text: One should have leaves of heman, that is gold, made thin and fine like birch bark.

children.text: tāni sūtena śuddhapāradena tulyāni khalve kṛtvā mardayet ||
children.translated_text: Having put them in a mortar with an equal quantity of sūta, purified mercury, one should triturate them.

children.text: kāñcanārastadrasena jvālāmukhī jayantī tadrasena vā lāṅgalyā kalihāryā vā rasena yāvat piṣṭikā bhavati tato hemnaścaturthāṃśaṃ ṭaṅkaṇaṃ saubhāgyapiṣṭamauktikacūrṇaṃ hema dviguṇam āvapet melayet teṣu sarvasamaṃ svarṇādisamaṃ gandhaṃ gandhakaṃ kṣipet śuddhaṃ teṣāṃ sarveṣāṃ golaṃ vāsobhirveṣṭayitvā śoṣayitvā ca dhārayet ||
children.translated_text: Kāñcanāra means with its juice; or with the juice of jvālāmukhī or jayantī, or with the juice of lāṅgalī or kalihārī, until a paste is formed. Then one should add ṭaṅkaṇa equal to a fourth part of the gold, powdered saubhāgya and pearl, and twice as much gold; mix them. Among these one should put purified gandha, sulfur, equal to all, that is equal to the gold and the rest. Having wrapped the bolus of all these in cloths and dried it, one should keep it.

children.text: kutra śarāvasaṃpuṭasya ante madhye tatra mudrāṃ pradāpayet lavaṇapūrite bhāṇḍe taṃ saṃpuṭaṃ dhārayet ||
children.translated_text: Where? In the interior, the middle, of a sealed saucer; there one should have a seal applied. One should keep that sealed container in a vessel filled with salt.

children.text: mudrāṃ dattvā śoṣayitvā bahubhirgomayaiḥ puṭet cullyāṃ vā agniṃ dāpayet tataḥ śīte samākṛṣya gandhasūtaṃ samaṃ golakaṃ samaṃ kṣipet pūrvavat khalve piṣṭvā gajapuṭe pacet svāṅgaśītaṃ guñjāyugmam atra yojayet ||
children.translated_text: After sealing and drying it, one should heat it with many cow-dung cakes, or apply fire on a stove. Then, when it is cool, one should take it out, add an equal bolus of gandha-sūta, pound it in a mortar as before, and cook it in a gajapuṭa. When it has cooled naturally, two guñjās should be used here.

children.text: aṣṭābhiḥ maricairvā tribhiḥ sarpiṣā ghṛtena madhunā vā doṣāpekṣayā deyā ||
children.translated_text: Or it should be given with eight peppers, or with three, with ghee or with honey, according to the doṣa.
The wholesome regimen is the same as for <s>Lokanātha</s>.

children.text: svacchamanāḥ punaḥ śuciḥ pavitro rogī ayaṃ mṛgāṅkaḥ śleṣmādīn hanyāt mṛgāṅkaścandras tannāmā mṛtāmayatvādroganāśakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The patient should again be clear-minded, pure, and clean. This <s>Mṛgāṅka</s> destroys phlegm and the others. Mṛgāṅka means the moon; this bears that name because, being deathless, it destroys disease.

children.text: yadvā pūrve mṛgāṅke ca kṣayarogatvāt pūrvaṃ dattastasmādayaṃ mṛgāṅkaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Or else, because in the earlier <s>Mṛgāṅka</s> it was formerly prescribed for wasting disease, therefore this is <s>Mṛgāṅka</s>.

children.text: kecit mṛtasvarṇena mṛtapāradena gaṃdhakaṃ ṭaṅkaṇaṃ muktācūrṇena mṛgāṅkasādhanamāhuḥ ||
children.translated_text: Some say that the preparation of <s>Mṛgāṅka</s> is made with incinerated gold, incinerated mercury, sulfur, borax, and pearl powder.
And that is as follows:
Gold reduced to ash, equal to mercury, and also equal to mercury through sulfur,

children.text: dinauktikaṃ pādikaṭaṅkaṇaṃ ca jambīranīre vaṭakīkṛtaṃ tat
children.translated_text: with daily pearl and a quarter part of borax, made into a pellet with citron juice:
when cooked in a vajra apparatus covered with burnt cloths, the said <s>Mṛgāṅka</s> conquers wasting disease.
Asureśa of the king of rasas means sulfur.
In another treatise it is described as <s>Kumudeśvara</s>.
And likewise:

children.text: hemabhasma rasabhasma mauktikaṃ pāradaṃ kaṇakagandhakaṃ ca kuru sarvatulyakam
children.translated_text: Make gold ash, mercury ash, pearl, mercury, kaṇaka-sulfur, all in equal quantity.

children.text: kāñjikena parimardya golakaṃ mūṣayā ca pariveṣṭya pācayet
children.translated_text: Having thoroughly triturated it with kāñjika and made a bolus, one should enclose it in a crucible and cook it.
Then one should take it out from the sealed container; the rasa called <s>Kumudeśvara</s> attains perfection.
When it has been drunk with kaṇas soaked in honey, one should then administer goat’s milk in the same way.
The wholesome regimen here is regarded as cool food cooked with ghee, without alkali or hiṅgu.

children.text: bhasmīkṛtasvarṇaṃ tolakaṃ mṛtapāradaṃ tolakaṃ mṛtamauktikaṃ tolakaṃ kāñjikena nimbūkena vā golaṃ kṛtvā mūṣābhyantare nirudhya lavaṇena pūrya haṇḍikāyāṃ madhye sthāpayitvā vahniṃ jvālayet ||
children.translated_text: Having made a bolus with one tolaka of incinerated gold, one tolaka of incinerated mercury, and one tolaka of incinerated pearl, using kāñjika or lemon, one should enclose it inside a crucible, fill it with salt, place it in the middle of a pot, and kindle the fire.
In the cold season one should eat one raktikā with honey.

children.text: chāgadugdhaṃ pibet pathyaṃ yathoktaṃ kumudeśvara eva mṛgāṅkaḥ ||
children.translated_text: One should drink goat's milk; the wholesome regimen is as stated. The very same <s>Kumudeśvara</s> is <s>Mṛgāṅka</s>.

children.text: rasasya śuddhapāradasya catvāro bhāgāḥ kanakasya svarṇasya tāvantaḥ spaṣṭamanyat ||
children.translated_text: Of the rasa, that is purified mercury, there are four parts; of kanaka, that is gold, just as many. The rest is clear.

children.text: śāṇasaṃmitaḥ ṭaṃkaṇapramāṇaḥ śuddhaṃ sūtaṃ viṣaṃ gandhaṃ ceti dhattūrabījaṃ triśāṇaṃ sarvebhyo dviguṇā dvādaśa bhāgā hemāhvā hemakṣīrī tasya sthāne vyoṣaṃ trikaṭurityeke ||
children.translated_text: Śāṇa-saṃmita means measured by śāṇas; ṭaṅkaṇa-pramāṇa means the measure of borax. Purified sūta, poison, and gandha, that is sulfur; dhattūra seed is three śāṇas; hemāhvā, that is hemakṣīrī, is twice all the others, twelve parts. Some say that in its place there is vyoṣa, that is trikaṭu.
The rest is clear.

children.text: daradaṃ hiṃgulaṃ vatsanābhaṃ viṣaṃ maricaṃ ṭaṅkaṇaṃ saubhāgyaṃ samabhāgaṃ cūrṇaṃ guñjaikaṃ deyam anupānaṃ kuṭajasya phalam indrayavaṃ tathā kuṭajatvacaṃ karṣamātraṃ madhunā deyaṃ gavyam ājyaṃ vā takram ||
children.translated_text: Darada, hiṅgula, vatsanābha poison, pepper, ṭaṅkaṇa, and saubhāgya are to be powdered in equal parts; one guñjā is to be given. As an adjuvant, the fruit of kuṭaja, namely indrayava, and likewise kuṭaja bark, in a karṣa measure, are to be given with honey, or with cow's ghee, or with buttermilk.
The rest is easy.
It is easy.
The juice of tālaparṇī and musalī should be given.
Or a decoction boiled with pañcakola should be given.
These are sannipāta conditions in which kapha is predominant.
It is easy.

children.text: nistvak tvacārahitaṃ jaipālaṃ daśaniṣkaṃ daśaṭaṅkaṃ maricaṃ pippalīmūlaṃ pāradaṃ gandhamūrchitaṃ pratiniṣkaṃ pratyekaṃ ṭaṅkam ||
children.translated_text: Jaipāla without its skin, that is without the bark, is ten niṣkas, ten ṭaṅkas; pepper, pippalī root, mercury stupefied with sulfur, each one niṣka, that is one ṭaṅka apiece.
For seven days, that is for seven days, it should be impregnated with liquids born from jambīra.

children.text: tadā vaṭī kāryā sā añjanena sannipātaṃ hanti ||
children.translated_text: Then pills should be made. That pill, used as a collyrium, destroys sannipāta.
Ṭaṅkaṇa means saubhāgya, and it is roasted.
The rest is easy.

children.text: daradaṃ hiṅgulaṃ hemāhvā cokapatramātraṃ hiṅgulādyāḥ karṣamātraṃ dantībījaṃ tatsamaṃ godugdhena triguñjaṃ pibet ||
children.translated_text: Darada, hiṅgula, hemāhvā, and a measure the size of a coka leaf; the hiṅgula and the others are a karṣa measure. Dantī seed is equal to that. One should drink three guñjās with cow's milk.
The rest is clear.
Now the rasa called <s>Rājamṛgāṅka</s>, for wasting disease and the like.

children.text: śilā manaḥśilā tālakaṃ haritālaṃ varāṭīḥ kapardikāstena pūrayet ||
children.translated_text: Śilā, that is manaḥśilā, tālaka, that is haritāla, and varāṭī shells, that is kapardikās: he should fill them with it.
Having ground ṭaṅkaṇa with goat's milk, he should seal the mouth.

children.text: punaḥ mṛdbhāṇḍe ruddhvā gajapuṭe pacet spaṣṭamanyat ||
children.translated_text: Then, having sealed it in an earthen vessel, he should cook it in a gajapuṭa. The rest is clear.

children.text: śuddhaṃ sūtaṃ pāradaṃ bhāgaikaṃ dvidhā dvibhāgaṃ gandhakaṃ tīkṣṇacūrṇaṃ dvayoḥ samaṃ tribhāgaṃ bhṛṅgajo bhṛṅgarājaḥ kākamācī prasiddhā kuraṇṭaḥ pītavāsā ||
children.translated_text: Purified sūta, that is mercury, is one part; in two portions, two parts of gandhaka; tīkṣṇa powder equal to the two; three parts. Bhṛṅgaja is bhṛṅgarāja; kākamācī is well known; kuraṇṭa is pītavāsā.

children.text: muṇḍī punarnavā sahadevī amṛtā guḍūcī nīlapuṣpī parājitā nirguṇḍī citraṃ citrakaṃ teṣāṃ dravaiḥ sapta sapta bhāvanā deyā ||
children.translated_text: Muṇḍī, punarnavā, sahadevī, amṛtā, that is guḍūcī, nīlapuṣpī, parājitā, nirguṇḍī, and citra, that is citraka: with the liquids of these, seven impregnations each should be given.
Elā, that is bṛhadelā, two niṣkas, and two ṭaṅkas, should be eaten.
In the sthālikā apparatus, that is in a double-pot sealed container, in the kayacī apparatus.

children.text: tāpyaṃ svarṇamākṣikaṃ śuddhaṃ pathyā harītakī agnimanthaḥ araṇī nirguṇḍī prasiddhā ṭaṅkaṇaṃ saubhāgyaṃ tacca bharjitaṃ viṣaṃ śuddhaṃ dviguñjaṃ bhakṣayet rāsnādikvāthānupānaṃ vā ||
children.translated_text: Tāpya, that is purified svarṇamākṣika; pathyā, that is harītakī; agnimantha, that is araṇī; nirguṇḍī, well known; ṭaṅkaṇa, that is saubhāgya, and that roasted; purified poison: one should eat two guñjās, or take a decoction of rāsnā and the rest as the adjuvant.
Vātāri means castor root.
It is easy.

children.text: mṛtaṃ tāmram ajākṣīraṃ tulyaṃ pācyaṃ tolakamitaṃ dugdhaṃ tulyād aṣṭaguṇam adhikaṃ deyam anyathā pākaḥ samyagbhavati ||
children.translated_text: Incinerated copper and goat's milk are to be cooked in equal quantity. Milk measured by the tolaka is to be given in eight times greater quantity than the equal amount; otherwise the cooking is not properly accomplished.

children.text: gatadravaistu tāmraṃ śuddhasūtaṃ gandhakaṃ ca samaṃ tolakaṃ vālukāyantre pācyam ||
children.translated_text: When the liquids have disappeared, copper, purified sūta, and sulfur, each equal to one tolaka, should be cooked in a sand apparatus.

children.text: haṇḍikāyāṃ golakaṃ sthāpya upari śarāvakaṃ dattvā mudrā deyā uparivālukāṃ dattvā mudrāṃ dāpayet ||
children.translated_text: Having placed the ball in a pot and put a saucer above it, a seal should be applied; after putting sand above it, he should have the seal applied.
This is the sand apparatus.
The remainder is easy.
Now the rasa called <s>Mahātāleśvara</s>, for kuṣṭha and the like.

children.text: tālaṃ haritālaṃ śuddhaṃ tāpyaṃ svarṇamākṣikaṃ śuddham ||
children.translated_text: Tāla, that is purified haritāla; tāpya, that is purified svarṇamākṣika.

children.text: śilā manaḥśilā sūtaṃ pāradaṃ saindhavaṃ ṭaṅkaṇaṃ saubhāgyaṃ bhūdhare kacchapayantre saṃpuṭe saṃpuṭodare śarāvasaṃpuṭamadhye etatsiddhaṃ rasaṃ ṣaṭpalaṃ gṛhītvā tatpaścādagnau melayet ||
children.translated_text: Śilā, that is manaḥśilā; sūta, that is mercury; saindhava; ṭaṅkaṇa, that is saubhāgya: in the bhūdhara, that is in the tortoise apparatus, in a sealed container, in the belly of the sealed container, in the middle of a sealed pair of saucers, this perfected rasa should be taken in a measure of six palas, and afterwards it should be fused in fire.

children.text: dvipalaṃ tāmraṃ catuḥpalaṃ lohabhasma jambīrāmlena mardyaṃ laghupuṭena vahnau saṃyojya triṃśadaṃśaṃ viṣaṃ melayet ||
children.translated_text: Two palas of copper and four palas of iron ash should be triturated with the acid juice of jambīra, joined with fire by means of a light puṭa, and mixed with poison in a thirtieth part.
With buffalo ghee, that is with the ghee of a she-buffalo, one should eat half a niṣka, that is half a ṭaṅka.
One should lick a karṣa measure of vākucī powder.

children.text: bhasmasūtaṃ mṛtaṃ pāradaṃ tatsamo gandhaḥ gandhakaṃ mṛtāyaḥ mṛtalohaṃ mṛtatāmraṃ gugguluḥ mahānimba iti citrakaḥ prasiddhaḥ śilājatusattvam etatpratyekaṃ ṣoḍaśaśāṇaṃ catuḥṣaṣṭiśāṇaṃ mṛtam abhraṃ sarvaṃ madhvājyābhyāṃ viloḍayet ||
children.translated_text: Ash-sūta means incinerated mercury; sulfur equal to it; mṛtāyas, that is incinerated iron; incinerated copper; guggulu; mahānimba, that is the well-known citraka; and the essence of śilājatu: each of these is sixteen śāṇas. Incinerated mica is sixty-four śāṇas. All of it should be mixed with honey and ghee.
Kept in a greased vessel, that is in a sticky vessel, one should eat it when it has been killed, that is incinerated.
Two niṣkas means one ṭaṅka.

children.text: piṭharīmadhye haṇḍikāmadhye tāmrapātreṇa sūtakāt triguṇena punaḥ adhomukhena pārśve tatpārśve bhasma utpalādijā jāritaṃ sthāpayet ||
children.translated_text: Inside a piṭharī, that is inside a pot, with a copper vessel three times larger than the sūtaka, again turned face down, at the side, and at its side, ash made from utpala and the like and subjected to jāraṇa should be placed.

children.text: upari pātraṃ dattvā mudrayitvā tadupari gomayaṃ jalaṃ kiṃcit pradātavyaṃ yāmadvayaṃ cullyāṃ pacet ||
children.translated_text: Having put a vessel above and sealed it, on top of that cow-dung water should be applied a little; it should be cooked on a hearth for two yāmas.
The rest is clear.

children.text: atha citralepaḥ guñjāphalam agniścitrakastaccūrṇaṃ lepitaṃ śvetakuṣṭhanudbhavati ||
children.translated_text: Now the variegated plaster: guñjā fruit and agni, that is citraka; when that powder is smeared on, it destroys white kuṣṭha.

children.text: śilā manaḥśilā apāmārgastadbhasmāpi liptaḥ śvitraṃ vināśayet ||
children.translated_text: Śilā, that is manaḥśilā, and apāmārga; when its ash also is smeared on, it destroys śvitra.

children.text: unmatto dhattūraḥ snuhī sehuṇḍabhedaḥ arkaḥ raviḥ viṣamuṣṭir mahānimbam ||
children.translated_text: Unmatta is dhattūra; snuhī is a variety of sehuṇḍa; arka is ravi; viṣamuṣṭi is mahānimba.
Hayāri is karavīra.

children.text: pratyekena auṣadharasena dinaṃ dinaṃ mardyam evaṃ saptadinaṃ mardyaṃ vastraveṣṭitaṃ tadgolaṃ vālukāyantragaṃ ca svedyaṃ pācyamityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: With each medicinal juice, day by day, it is to be triturated; having triturated it in this way for seven days, that bolus, wrapped in cloth, should be placed in a sand apparatus and steamed, that is, cooked.
Devakāṣṭha is devadāru; the rest is clear.
Hemāhvā is svarṇakṣīrī; mūrchita sūta means mercury that has been stupefied.
The rest is clear.
Bhasmasūta is dead, incinerated mercury; kāntaloha is magnetic iron; muṇḍa too is a particular kind of iron.

children.text: tāpyaṃ śilā manaḥśilā vyoṣaṃ trikaṭu triphalā kolabījaṃ kapittham ||
children.translated_text: Tāpya is śilā; manaḥśilā is realgar; vyoṣa is trikaṭu; triphalā; kolabīja is kapittha.

children.text: etatsarvaṃ tulyaṃ bhṛṅgarājena ekaviṃśatirbhāvayet niṣkaṃ ṭaṅkamātraṃ madhuyuktaṃ lihet ||
children.translated_text: All this, in equal quantity, should be impregnated twenty-one times with bhṛṅgarāja; one should lick a niṣka, that is a ṭaṅka measure, mixed with honey.
The rest is clear.

children.text: atha vahniraso jalodarādau śivā harītakī dviguṇā punaruktatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Now, in the Vahnirasa for dropsy and the like, śivā is harītakī; it is doubled because it is mentioned again.

children.text: trivṛt nisotaḥ dantībījaṃ jaipālaṃ citrakaṃ prasiddham etat tribhāgaṃ pratyekam ||
children.translated_text: Trivṛt is nisota; dantībīja is jaipāla; citraka is well known; each of these is three parts.

children.text: tryūṣaṇaṃ trikaṭu dantī jaṭā jīrakaṃ pratyekamaṣṭabhāgaṃ jayantī śākaviśeṣaḥ snuk sehuṇḍadugdhaṃ bhṛṅgaṃ mārkavaḥ vahniścitrakaḥ vātāritailam eraṇḍatailaṃ pratyekena rasena saptasaptavāraṃ bhāvyam ||
children.translated_text: Tryūṣaṇa is trikaṭu; dantī, jaṭā, and jīraka are each eight parts; jayantī is a particular vegetable; snuk is sehuṇḍa milk; bhṛṅga is mārkava; vahni is citraka; vātāri oil is castor oil. It should be impregnated seven times each with the individual juices.
Vajrī is sehuṇḍa.
The remainder is easy to understand.

children.text: ṭaṅkaṇaṃ saubhāgyaṃ hāriṇaṃ śṛṅgaṃ svarṇaṃ mṛtaṃ śuddhaṃ tāmraṃ mṛtaṃ ruddhvā śarāvasaṃpuṭe vanopalaiḥ pacet ||
children.translated_text: Ṭaṅkaṇa is saubhāgya; hāriṇa is horn; svarṇa means gold, incinerated and purified; tāmra means copper, incinerated. Having sealed it in a saucer container, one should cook it with forest cow-dung cakes.
The rest is clear.
It is easy to understand.

children.text: vahniścitrakaḥ viṣamuṣṭiḥ mahānimbaphalaṃ kucelaṃ vā dvayorabhāve samudraphalaṃ vā deyam ||
children.translated_text: Vahni is citraka; viṣamuṣṭi is the fruit of mahānimba, or kucela; if both are unavailable, samudraphala may be given.
It is easy to understand.

children.text: tālaṃ haritālaṃ kaṭukī etatsamaṃ mṛtasūtādyam aṣṭauṣadhaṃ cūrṇitam ebhiḥ punarnavādibhirbhāvayet ||
children.translated_text: Tāla is haritāla; kaṭukī: an equal quantity of this and the eight medicines beginning with incinerated mercury, powdered, should be impregnated with these plants beginning with punarnavā.

children.text: punarnavā varṣābhūḥ devadālī nirguṇḍī taṇḍulīyakaṃ meghanādaḥ tiktakośātakī jālinī eṣāṃ drāvairdinaikaṃ mardayet ||
children.translated_text: Punarnavā is varṣābhū; devadālī, nirguṇḍī, taṇḍulīyaka, meghanāda, tiktakośātakī, and jālinī: with the liquids of these one should triturate it for one day.
Then one should triturate it with milk.
One should lick a māṣa measure with honey, and afterward drink a decoction of neem leaves.
Or one should induce vomiting with a tube of castor plant.
Diseases such as phlegm-wasting and cough disappear.

children.text: sūtaṃ mṛtaṃ pāradaṃ hāṭakaṃ svarṇaṃ vajraṃ hīrakaṃ mṛtamabhrakaṃ vā lohaṃ mākṣikaṃ svarṇamākṣikaṃ tālaṃ haritālaṃ nīlāñjanaṃ tutthaṃ śuddhaṃ māritaṃ tadabhāve tāmraṃ vā deyaṃ vamanabhayāt ||
children.translated_text: Sūta means incinerated mercury; pārada means mercury; hāṭaka means gold; vajra means diamond; incinerated abhraka, or iron, mākṣika, svarṇamākṣika, tāla, haritāla, nīlāñjana, and tuttha, purified and killed, are to be used; in its absence, copper may be given, because of fear of vomiting.
Ahiphena is aphūka; this, in equal quantity, should be thoroughly triturated with vajrakṣāras.

children.text: kanakasya dhattūrabījasya aṣṭa śāṇāḥ aṣṭa ṭaṅkāḥ sūtaḥ śuddhaḥ dvādaśa ṭaṅkaḥ tāmraṃ mṛtaṃ dviśāṇam abhrakaṃ catuḥśāṇaṃ mākṣikaṃ mṛtaṃ dviśāṇaṃ vaṅgo mṛtaḥ dviśāṇaḥ sauvīraḥ añjanaṃ triśāṇaṃ lohaṃ mṛtam aṣṭaśāṇam ||
children.translated_text: Of kanaka, that is dhattūra seed, eight śāṇas, that is eight ṭaṅkas; purified mercury, twelve ṭaṅkas; incinerated copper, two śāṇas; abhraka, four śāṇas; incinerated mākṣika, two śāṇas; incinerated vaṅga, two śāṇas; sauvīra añjana, three śāṇas; and incinerated iron, eight śāṇas.

children.text: viṣaṃ triśāṇaṃ lāṅgalī kalihārī palapramāṇā amlavetasādyaiḥ mṛdupuṭaṃ dadyāt ||
children.translated_text: Viṣa, three śāṇas; lāṅgalī, that is kalihārī, in a pala measure. With amlavetasa and the like, one should give a mild puṭa heating.
Again, a māṣa measure is to be given.

children.text: ārdrakarasena rasonarasena vā kilāsaṃ citrakuṣṭhāni visarpabhagandaraṃ jvaraṃ viṣam ajīrṇaṃ jayet etadrogaharo rasaḥ kanakasundaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: With ginger juice or garlic juice it conquers kilāsa, spotted leprosy, erysipelas, fistula, fever, poison, and indigestion. This disease-destroying rasa is <s>Kanakasundara</s>.

children.text: pāradaḥ gandhakaḥ trikarṣau etau mṛtaṃ tāraṃ mṛtaṃ rūpyam ||
children.translated_text: Pārada and gandhaka are each three karṣas; these two, and dead tāra, that is incinerated silver.

children.text: abhraṃ abhrakaṃ vaṅgaṃ ahiḥ nāgaṃ sāraṃ lohaṃ ete ekaikakarṣakāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Abhra means abhraka; vaṅga; ahi is nāga; sāra is iron; these are one karṣa each.

children.text: śigru śobhāñjanam jvālāmukhī jayantī taṇḍulīyakaḥ ebhir golakaṃ kṛtvā punarvastrairghṛtaṃ kācapātrasthaṃ lavaṇapūrite bhāṇḍe nyaset ||
children.translated_text: Śigru is śobhāñjana; jvālāmukhī, jayantī, and taṇḍulīyaka: having made a bolus with these, again smeared with cloths, it should be placed in a glass vessel inside a pot filled with salt.
One should apply fire.
For two yāmas.

children.text: tataḥ punaḥ pravālacūrṇakarṣeṇa śāṇamātraviṣeṇa melayitvā kṛṣṇasarpasya garalairbhāvayet divasamekaṃ dinaṃ paścātsthālikāyāṃ haṇḍikāyāṃ ca kupīṃ niveśayet ||
children.translated_text: Then again, after mixing it with a karṣa of coral powder and a śāṇa measure of poison, one should impregnate it with the venom of a black snake for one day; after a day, one should set the bottle in an earthen cooking pot and a small pot.

children.text: hemāhvā svarṇakṣīrī nīlinī aparājitā kuṭherakaḥ śvetatulasī devadālī ||
children.translated_text: Hemāhvā is svarṇakṣīrī; nīlinī, aparājitā, kuṭheraka, white tulasī, and devadālī.

children.text: madhūkaṃ guḍapuṣpaṃ jātī mālatī madanaphalaṃ spaṣṭamanyat ||
children.translated_text: Madhūka is guḍapuṣpa; jātī, mālatī, and madanaphala; the rest is clear.

children.text: tāraṃ raupyaṃ mṛtaṃ mauktikaṃ muktāphalaṃ hema svarṇaṃ mṛtaṃ sāro mṛtalohaḥ ete pratyekabhāgikāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Tāra is silver, incinerated; mauktika is pearl; hema is gold, incinerated; sāra is incinerated iron. These are each one part.
Gandha is two parts; sūta is mercury, purified, three parts.
Having made these into kajjalī, triturated them with the fresh juice of kapittha fruit, one should place them in a deer's horn.
After applying a clay cloth covering, one should heat it in a medium puṭa.

children.text: balā prasiddhā tadrasaiḥ saptavelaṃ saptavāraṃ bhāvayet ||
children.translated_text: Balā is well known; with its juices one should impregnate it seven times.
Apāmārga is ūrdhvakaṇṭaka; with its juices one should impregnate it three times.

children.text: lodhraṃ prasiddhaṃ prativiṣā ativiṣā mustaṃ nāgaraṃ dhātakīpuṣpāṇi indrayavaḥ amṛtā guḍūcī eṣāṃ svarasaiḥ pratyekaṃ tridhā bhāvanā syāt ||
children.translated_text: Lodhra is well known; prativiṣā is ativiṣā; musta, nāgara, dhātakī flowers, indrayava, amṛtā, and guḍūcī: with the fresh juices of these, each separately, there should be three impregnations.
When perfected through those beginning with that, a māṣa measure is to be given.

children.text: madhunā tathā maricairapi māṣamātraiḥ sarvānatīsārān tathā sarvajāṃ grahaṇīṃ hanyāt ||
children.translated_text: With honey, and also with peppers in māṣa measures, it destroys all forms of diarrhea and every kind of grahaṇī disease.

children.text: mṛtasūtaṃ mṛtapāradaṃ abhrakaṃ gandhakaṃ yavakṣāraṃ saubhāgyaṃ agnimantho vacā etāni sūtatulyāni kuryāt ||
children.translated_text: Incinerated sūta, incinerated mercury, abhraka, sulfur, yavakṣāra, saubhāgya, agnimantha, and vacā: these should be made equal to the sūta.
Each part is regarded as equal to the amount of sūta.
Then one should triturate it with jayantī and the other juices.

children.text: trivāsaraṃ tridinaṃ tato golaṃ kṛtvā saṃśoṣya lohapātre kaṭāhikādau dhṛtvā upari śarāvaṃ dattvā mudrayet ||
children.translated_text: For trivāsara, that is for three days, then having made it into a bolus, dried it thoroughly, and placed it in an iron vessel such as a pan, one should put a saucer over it and seal it.
One should apply fire gently for half a yāma.

children.text: golakatulyāṃ prativiṣāṃ tathā mocarasaṃ dattvā kapitthādibhiḥ saptasapta bhāvayet ||
children.translated_text: Having added prativiṣā equal to the bolus, and likewise mocarasa, one should give seven bhāvanās each with kapittha and the other juices.

children.text: vijayā bhaṅgā kapitthaṃ prasiddhaṃ tairdhātakyādibhirvāraikaṃ bhāvayet ||
children.translated_text: Vijayā means bhaṅgā; kapittha is well known. With these, or with dhātakī and the others, one should give one bhāvanā.

children.text: dhātakīpuṣpāṇi indrayavaḥ mustaṃ lodhraṃ bilvaṃ guḍūcī etaiḥ śāṇaṃ ṭaṅkaṃ madhunā lihet ||
children.translated_text: Dhātakī flowers, indrayava, musta, lodhra, bilva, and guḍūcī: with these, one śāṇa or ṭaṅka should be licked with honey.

children.text: vahniścitrakaṃ śuṇṭhī biḍaṃ biḍalavaṇaṃ saindhavaṃ etadanupānaṃ pibet ||
children.translated_text: Vahni means citraka; śuṇṭhī, biḍa, biḍa-lavaṇa, and saindhava: one should drink this as the accompanying drink.

children.text: tāraṃ raupyaṃ mṛtaṃ vajraṃ hīrakaṃ abhrakaṃ vā suvarṇaṃ mṛtaṃ gandhakaṃ sūtakaṃ śuddhaṃ tīkṣṇaṃ etāni kramavṛddhāni tāraṃ bhāgaikaṃ vajraṃ dvibhāgaṃ suvarṇaṃ tribhāgaṃ tāmraṃ caturbhāgaṃ sūtaṃ saptabhāgaṃ lohamaṣṭabhāgaṃ evaṃ arkadugdhairmardya kācakupyāṃ vālukāyantre pācayet ||
children.translated_text: Tāra is silver, incinerated; vajra means diamond, or abhraka; suvarṇa is incinerated gold; gandhaka is sulfur; sūtaka is purified mercury; tīkṣṇa is iron. These are increased in order: one part of tāra, two parts of vajra, three parts of gold, four parts of copper, seven parts of mercury, and eight parts of iron. Thus, having triturated them with arka milk, one should cook them in a glass bottle in a sand apparatus.
Then, having triturated it with aśvagandhā and the other substances, one should eat it.

children.text: arkadugdhaṃ yadyapi bhāvanādravye likhitaṃ tathāpi kumāryā sahaiva deyaṃ arkadugdhasya bhakṣaṇānucitatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Although arka milk is written among the liquids for bhāvanā, still it should be given only together with kumārī, because arka milk is not suitable for eating.

children.text: vānarī kapikacchūḥ muśalī ikṣurā tālamūlī spaṣṭamanyat ||
children.translated_text: Vānarī means kapikacchū; muśalī, ikṣurā, and tālamūlī are clear, as is the rest.
Now, <s>Kandarpasundara rasa</s>.

children.text: sūtaḥ pāradaḥ vajraṃ hīrakaṃ vā abhrakaṃ ahiḥ sīsakaḥ muktā prasiddhā tāraṃ raupyaṃ mṛtaṃ hema svarṇaṃ mṛtaṃ sitābhrakaṃ śvetābhrakaṃ māritam etān karṣāṃśikān pratyekān irimedo viṭkhadiraḥ tena mardayet ||
children.translated_text: Sūta is mercury; vajra means diamond, or abhraka; ahiḥ is lead; muktā is well known; tāra is silver, incinerated; hema is gold, incinerated; sitābhraka is white mica, killed. These, each in the measure of a karṣa, should be triturated with irimeda, that is viṭkhadira.
Pravāla is coral, two karṣas; gandhaka is sulfur, two karṣas.
It should be triturated with the fresh juice of aśvagandhā, placed in a deer horn, and cooked with a mild puṭa.
Then one should give bhāvanā with the juice of dhātakī.

children.text: parūṣakaphalaviśeṣaḥ kaseruḥ prasiddhaḥ madhūkaṃ guḍapuṣpaḥ vānarī kapikacchūḥ eṣāṃ rasairbhāvayitvā śoṣayitvā vicūrṇayet ||
children.translated_text: Parūṣaka is a particular fruit; kaseru is well known; madhūka is guḍapuṣpa; vānarī is kapikacchū. Having given bhāvanā with the juices of these, dried it, one should pulverize it.
One should mix it with elā and the other ingredients, each in the measure of a śāṇa.

children.text: punaḥ kandarpasundaraṃ śāṇamitaṃ rātrau sitā dhātrī vidārikā eteṣāṃ karṣacūrṇena yutaṃ sarpiḥkarṣeṇa saṃyutaṃ khādet ||
children.translated_text: Again, at night one should eat <s>Kandarpasundara</s> in a śāṇa measure, joined with a karṣa of powder of sitā, dhātrī, and vidārikā, and combined with a karṣa of ghee.
After it, one should drink two palas of milk.
With a very steady mind, he should delight a beautiful woman.

children.text: elā kṣudrailā patraṃ patrajaṃ vāṃśī rocanā lavaṅgaṃ agaru kesaraṃ mustaṃ mṛgamadaṃ kastūrī kṛṣṇā pippalī jalaṃ vālakaṃ candraḥ karpūraḥ sitā prasiddhā dhātrī āmalakī vidārīkandaṃ sarpirghṛtaṃ spaṣṭam anyat ||
children.translated_text: Elā is lesser cardamom; patra means patraja; vāṃśī, rocanā, lavaṅga, agaru, kesara, musta, mṛgamada, kastūrī, kṛṣṇā pippalī, jala, vālaka, candra, that is camphor, sitā is well known, dhātrī is āmalakī, vidārīkanda, and sarpis is ghee; the rest is clear.

children.text: śuddhaṃ rasendraṃ bhāgaikaṃ dvibhāgaṃ gandhakaṃ śuddhaṃ tayoḥ kajjalikāṃ kṛtvā tatra tīkṣṇabhavaṃ cūrṇaṃ sarvatulyaṃ kanyādrāvairmardayet tato golakaṃ kṛtvā eraṇḍapatrairveṣṭayitvā tāmrasampuṭe dhānyarāśau sthāpayet tataḥ kuṭhāracchinnādyair bhāvayet ||
children.translated_text: Taking one part of purified rasendra and two parts of purified sulfur, one should make kajjalikā from the two. Into that, one should add powder produced from tīkṣṇa, equal to the whole, and triturate with the fluids of kanyā. Then, having made a bolus, wrapped it in castor leaves, put it in a copper sealed container, and placed it in a heap of grain, one should then give bhāvanā with kuṭhārachinnā and the other substances.

children.text: kuṭhārachinnā bisaṃ mṛṇālaṃ bhṛṅgo bhṛṅgarājaḥ kuraṇṭakaḥ pītavāsā nīlikā aparājitā alambuṣā muṇḍī varī śatāvarī ||
children.translated_text: Kuṭhārachinnā means bisa, the lotus fiber; bhṛṅga means bhṛṅgarāja; kuraṇṭaka, pītavāsā, nīlikā, aparājitā, alambuṣā, muṇḍī, varī, and śatāvarī.
